title: What accounting is and why businesses need it

scenes.kicker: F01 · Introduction to Financial Accounting · Module 1
scenes.head: What accounting is and why businesses need it
scenes.sub: Accounting turns what happens to a business into information that owners, lenders, investors and governments can act on. Learn who relies on that information, the four statements it produces, who writes the rules, and the concepts that make the numbers worth trusting.

segs.say: What accounting is and why businesses need it. Accounting turns what happens to a business into information that owners, lenders, investors and governments can act on. Learn who relies on that information, the four statements it produces, who writes the rules, and the concepts that make the numbers worth trusting.

scenes.head: You will be able to

segs.say: Explain accounting as an information system that identifies, records and communicates the economic events of a business.
Identify the main users of accounting information and the decisions each one makes with it.
Distinguish financial, managerial and tax accounting by their users, rules and purpose.
Describe the question each of the four financial statements answers.
Explain who sets accounting standards in the United States and internationally, and what the conceptual framework is for.
Apply the qualitative characteristics, the four basic assumptions and the basic principles to everyday reporting decisions.

scenes.head: On 1 March 2026 Ana Lim opens Lantern Coffee Co., a small corporation that caters coffee for offices and events and runs barista-training workshops.

segs.say: On 1 March 2026 Ana Lim opens Lantern Coffee Co., a small corporation that caters coffee for offices and events and runs barista-training workshops. She puts in $20,000 of her savings, and Coastline Bank lends the company another $10,000. Within a week Lantern has bought an espresso machine, paid for a year of insurance, ordered beans and cups, and taken a deposit from its first corporate client. Ana now faces a question every founder meets: what does she need to write down, and for whom? She wants to know whether the business is making money. The bank wants to know whether it will be repaid. The tax authority will want to know how much tax Lantern owes. All of them need information about the same events, and none of them can see inside Lantern’s bank account and invoices for themselves.

scenes.head: Accounting is the system that turns those events into information people can use.

segs.say: Accounting is the system that turns those events into information people can use. It does three things. It identifies the economic events that belong to the business: buying the espresso machine counts, while a friendly conversation with a possible client does not, and neither does Ana’s personal grocery shopping. It records each event in money, with a date and a description, and sorts it so that similar events can be added up. And it communicates the results, in reports and financial statements, to the people who need them. Accounting, in short, is an information system that identifies, records and communicates the economic events of an organisation to the people who make decisions about it.

Accounting is the process of organizing, analyzing, and communicating financial information that is used for decision-making. (Franklin, Graybeal and Cooper, Principles of Accounting, Volume 1: Financial Accounting (OpenStax, 2019), section 1.1)

scenes.head: Recording is the part most people picture, and on its own it is called bookkeeping.

segs.say: Recording is the part most people picture, and on its own it is called bookkeeping. Accounting is wider: it decides what should be recorded and how, checks that the records are complete, and interprets them. A bookkeeper can tell Ana that Lantern spent $1,200 on kitchen rent in March; an accountant can help her decide whether the business can afford a second kitchen.

scenes.head: Different people read the same records to make different decisions.

segs.say: Different people read the same records to make different decisions. It helps to sort them into two groups. Internal users run the business: owners who manage it, like Ana, and the managers and staff who plan, price and control its work. External users are outside it and see only what the business chooses, or is required, to show them.
Users of accounting information and the decisions they make

scenes.head: For Lantern, three of these users matter from the first month.

segs.say: For Lantern, three of these users matter from the first month. Ana, as owner and manager, needs to know which of her two lines of business, catering or training, earns more. Coastline Bank needs to know whether Lantern can pay the interest due every three months and repay the $10,000 within the note’s two-year term. And the tax authority (the Internal Revenue Service in the United States) will expect a tax return.

scenes.head: Because the users differ, accounting has grown into three main branches.

segs.say: Because the users differ, accounting has grown into three main branches. Financial accounting produces general-purpose reports for people outside the business, chiefly investors and lenders, following a common set of rules so that readers can trust and compare them. Managerial accounting (also called management accounting) produces whatever internal reports help managers plan and control the business: budgets, the cost of each catering event, the profit on each workshop. It follows no external rule book and freely mixes money with other measures, such as the number of events catered each week. Tax accounting applies tax law to work out taxable income and the tax due. Its rules come from legislation and the tax authority, not from accounting standard setters, so taxable income and accounting profit often differ.
The three branches compared

scenes.head: The branches draw on the same records, but they can give different answers.

segs.say: The branches draw on the same records, but they can give different answers. Under US tax rules a business can elect to deduct the full cost of certain equipment in the year it starts using it (the section 179 deduction), while its financial statements spread that cost over the years the equipment is used. Neither figure is wrong: they answer different questions under different rules. This course is about financial accounting.

chapters.title: The four financial statements at a glance

scenes.head: Financial accounting communicates mainly through financial statements: structured reports that summarise what happened to a business during a period…

segs.say: Financial accounting communicates mainly through financial statements: structured reports that summarise what happened to a business during a period and where it stands at the end of it. A complete set has four main statements, each answering a different question, plus notes that explain them. You will prepare all four in lesson 10. For now, see what each is for, using the figures Lantern will report for March once its books are complete.
What each statement answers, with Lantern’s figures for March 2026 (fictional)

scenes.head: Two things stand out already.

segs.say: Two things stand out already. The income statement and the statement of cash flows cover a period (the month of March), while the balance sheet is a snapshot at one moment (the end of 31 March). And profit is not cash: Lantern earned $990 in March, yet its cash rose by $26,650, mostly because Ana and the bank put money in. Telling those two stories apart is one of the main reasons accounting exists.

scenes.head: One set of events, many questions

segs.say: One set of events, many questions. Accounting does not make decisions; it supplies the information for them. The same March events tell Ana whether catering pays, tell the bank whether its loan is safe and tell the tax authority what is owed.

scenes.head: Outsiders can rely on financial statements only if businesses prepare them in a consistent way, so reporting in each jurisdiction follows an agreed…

segs.say: Outsiders can rely on financial statements only if businesses prepare them in a consistent way, so reporting in each jurisdiction follows an agreed body of rules, called generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP). This lesson introduces two standard setters: the American one and the international one.

scenes.head: In the United States the rules are written by the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB), an independent, private-sector, not-for-profit…

segs.say: In the United States the rules are written by the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB), an independent, private-sector, not-for-profit organisation established in 1973 and based in Norwalk, Connecticut. Its standards are collected in the FASB Accounting Standards Codification, the source of authoritative US GAAP for nongovernmental entities: public and private companies and not-for-profit organisations.

scenes.head: The FASB’s authority over public companies comes through the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the federal agency that protects investors in…

segs.say: The FASB’s authority over public companies comes through the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the federal agency that protects investors in US securities markets. Under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 the SEC requires periodic reports from companies whose securities are publicly traded, and the securities laws let it set the accounting standards those reports use. Rather than write them itself, it recognises the FASB as the designated standard setter for public companies, a status it reaffirmed in 2003. A private company such as Lantern files nothing with the SEC, but its bank or a future investor may ask for GAAP statements, so Lantern keeps its books under US GAAP.

scenes.head: Many other jurisdictions use International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS), formally IFRS Accounting Standards, which are written by the…

segs.say: Many other jurisdictions use International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS), formally IFRS Accounting Standards, which are written by the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB). The IASB is an independent standard-setting body within the IFRS Foundation, a not-for-profit, public interest organisation that set up the IASB in 2001. Each jurisdiction decides whether to adopt them: the IFRS Foundation reports that companies in more than 140 jurisdictions are required to use them, but which companies must use them, and which merely may, varies. In the United States, the SEC requires domestic public companies to use US GAAP. Since a rule issued in December 2007, it has accepted statements prepared under IFRS as issued by the IASB from foreign private issuers (foreign companies whose securities trade in the United States), without a reconciliation to US GAAP.

scenes.head: US GAAP and IFRS in this course

segs.say: US GAAP and IFRS in this course. The mechanics this course teaches (the accounting equation, double-entry recording and the accounting cycle) are the same under both sets of standards. They differ in vocabulary and in many detailed rules for recognising and measuring particular items; where a difference matters here, a box like this one says so.

scenes.head: Standards on individual topics, such as leases or revenue, rest on a shared foundation called a conceptual framework: a set of concepts that says…

segs.say: Standards on individual topics, such as leases or revenue, rest on a shared foundation called a conceptual framework: a set of concepts that says what financial reporting is for and what makes information useful. Standard setters use it to keep their standards consistent with one another. Under IFRS, companies also use it to develop an accounting policy when no standard covers a transaction. The FASB’s framework is its Concepts Statement No. 8, issued in chapters, among them the objective and the qualitative characteristics in September 2010, at the end of a joint project with the IASB, and the elements of financial statements in December 2021. The IASB issued its current Conceptual Framework in March 2018. The two agree on most of what follows; the boxes note where they part.

scenes.head: Both frameworks start from the same objective.

segs.say: Both frameworks start from the same objective. The FASB states it this way, and the IASB’s paragraph 1.2 is worded almost identically:

The objective of general purpose financial reporting is to provide financial information about the reporting entity that is useful to existing and potential investors, lenders, and other creditors in making decisions about providing resources to the entity. (FASB Concepts Statement No. 8, Chapter 1, paragraph OB2)

scenes.head: Three phrases carry the weight.

segs.say: Three phrases carry the weight. General purpose means the reports are designed for many readers at once rather than tailored to one. Existing and potential investors, lenders and other creditors are the primary users, because they provide the business with money and many of them cannot insist on private reports. Decisions about providing resources covers buying, selling or holding shares and debt, making and settling loans and, the IASB adds, voting on or otherwise influencing how management uses the business’s resources. Both frameworks admit that such reports cannot give users everything they need; users also draw on other sources, such as the state of the economy and the industry.

chapters.title: What makes information useful: the qualitative characteristics

scenes.head: The frameworks name the qualities that make financial information useful.

segs.say: The frameworks name the qualities that make financial information useful. Two are fundamental, and information must have both. Four are enhancing: they make relevant, faithfully represented information more useful, but they cannot rescue information that lacks the fundamental two.

Relevance. Information is relevant if it is capable of making a difference to users’ decisions. It does so through predictive value (it helps users form expectations, as March’s catering revenue helps Ana and the bank estimate April’s), confirmatory value (it confirms or corrects earlier expectations), or both.

Materiality. Information is material if leaving it out or misstating it could change or influence the decisions of the people relying on the report. Whether something is material depends on the size and the nature of the item in one particular business, so no single dollar threshold fits every business.

Faithful representation. Information faithfully represents what it claims to describe if it is complete (nothing a user needs is left out), neutral (not slanted, by the choice of figures or how they are presented, to create a favourable or unfavourable impression) and free from error (no errors or omissions in the description, and a sound process behind any estimate). Free from error does not mean perfectly precise: an estimate, such as how many years the espresso machine will last, can be represented faithfully if it is made with care and clearly described as an estimate.

scenes.head: Materiality: two framings

segs.say: Materiality: two framings. The IASB calls materiality an entity-specific aspect of relevance, based on the nature or size of an item in one entity’s report, and says no uniform numerical threshold can be set. The FASB, after amending its framework in August 2018, keeps the two apart: relevance is a general notion about what type of information is useful, while materiality is entity specific, judged by whether the item is large enough, in the circumstances, that the judgement of a reasonable person relying on the report would probably have been changed or influenced. Neither thinks one materiality rule can fit every business.

scenes.head: Materiality is why accountants don’t chase every cent.

segs.say: Materiality is why accountants don’t chase every cent. If Lantern’s bookkeeper misfiled a $3 roll of tape, no reader’s decision would change. But materiality is measured against the reader’s decision, not against the number alone. A $150 error would be trivial for a hotel group earning millions and large for Lantern, whose March profit is $990: about 15% of it. In practice accountants and auditors often begin with a percentage rule of thumb, such as 5% of profit, and the SEC’s staff accepts such a rule as an initial step, but only as the beginning of the analysis. A small error can still be material because of its nature: for example, if it turns a loss into a profit, masks a change in a trend, affects whether a business complies with a loan agreement, or conceals an unlawful transaction (SEC Staff Accounting Bulletin No. 99, 1999).
The four enhancing qualitative characteristics

scenes.head: Both frameworks also recognise a constraint: cost.

segs.say: Both frameworks also recognise a constraint: cost. Information costs time and money to prepare, check and read, and the cost should be justified by the benefit. That is why a small business would sensibly record a $40 milk jug as an expense when it buys it instead of tracking it for years as it does an espresso machine.

scenes.head: Prudence and conservatism: the frameworks disagree

segs.say: Prudence and conservatism: the frameworks disagree. Many introductory texts, OpenStax’s among them, describe a principle of conservatism: when in doubt, choose the figure that makes assets and profit lower. The FASB’s framework leaves prudence and conservatism out of faithful representation, because a deliberate lean in either direction conflicts with neutrality. The IASB’s 2018 framework reintroduced prudence, defined as caution when making judgements under uncertainty, and says it supports neutrality: assets and income should not be overstated, nor liabilities and expenses understated, but assets and income may not be deliberately understated either, because that only shifts profit into later periods.

scenes.head: Textbooks gather the starting points of financial accounting into four assumptions.

segs.say: Textbooks gather the starting points of financial accounting into four assumptions. Each one shapes what Lantern records.

Economic entity assumption. The business is treated as separate from its owners and from every other business, and its records contain only its own events. Ana’s savings account, her car and her mortgage are not Lantern’s, and if Lantern pays one of Ana’s personal bills, that is not a business expense. The assumption applies to a one-owner business too, even though the law does not separate a sole proprietor from her business.

Going concern assumption. Unless there is evidence to the contrary, the business is expected to keep operating for the foreseeable future. That is why Lantern records its espresso machine at cost and spreads that cost over the five years it expects to use it, instead of reporting what the machine would fetch in a forced sale tomorrow. If a business intends or is forced to stop trading, its statements may have to be prepared on a different basis, and they must say so.

Monetary unit assumption. Only events that can be measured in money are recorded, in one currency (US dollars for Lantern), and the currency is treated as a stable unit, so changes in its purchasing power through inflation are ignored. A loyal clientele or a talented barista may be valuable, but neither appears in Lantern’s accounts.

Time period assumption. The life of a business can be divided into artificial periods (months, quarters, years) so that results can be reported while they are still useful. In this course Lantern prepares statements every month so that you can see a whole cycle; most businesses produce monthly figures for their managers but close their books formally once a year, at the end of a twelve-month fiscal year that need not end on 31 December.

scenes.head: Going concern under US GAAP and IFRS

segs.say: Going concern under US GAAP and IFRS. Both sets of standards require management to assess whether the going concern basis still holds when it prepares statements. Under US GAAP, management evaluates whether there is substantial doubt about the entity’s ability to meet its obligations as they fall due within one year after the date the statements are issued (or available to be issued). Under IFRS, management looks at least twelve months ahead from the end of the reporting period, and further where needed; these requirements move unchanged from IAS 1 to IAS 8 when IFRS 18 takes effect for periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027.

scenes.head: On top of the assumptions, four principles govern how events are recorded.

segs.say: On top of the assumptions, four principles govern how events are recorded. Lesson 8 studies two of them in depth; here is what each says.

Historical cost. Under the historical cost principle, assets are recorded at what they cost to acquire: the price paid plus the costs of getting them ready for use. Lantern’s espresso machine and grinder enter the records at $12,000, and stay there even if a similar machine soon costs more or a buyer offers less. Cost is verifiable, since there is an invoice, but it can drift away from current value, which is why the standards require current values for some items, such as certain investments.

Revenue recognition. Revenue is recorded when the business delivers the goods or services it promised, not when cash arrives. Lantern earns $4,200 when it caters Meridian Partners’ conference on 12 March, although it is paid later; Harbor Tech’s $2,400 deposit is not revenue until the events take place.

Expense recognition. Expenses are recorded in the period in which resources are used up to earn revenue (often summarised as matching expenses with revenue), not when they are paid for. Lantern’s $1,800 insurance policy becomes an expense at $150 a month over the year it covers.

Full disclosure. Under the full disclosure principle, the statements and their notes should include everything a reader needs to understand them: the accounting methods used, the terms of a bank loan, a lawsuit filed against the business, a major event after the end of the period. The notes are part of the financial statements, not an optional extra.

scenes.head: Financial statements are prepared by the managers whose performance they describe, which gives managers a reason to flatter the numbers.

segs.say: Financial statements are prepared by the managers whose performance they describe, which gives managers a reason to flatter the numbers. Two safeguards make the statements credible. The first is an audit: an independent accountant examines the records and the evidence behind them and gives an opinion on whether the statements present the business’s financial position and results fairly, in all material respects, in accordance with the applicable framework, such as US GAAP or IFRS. Public companies in the United States must be audited, and since the Sarbanes–Oxley Act of 2002, passed to combat corporate and accounting fraud, their auditors have been overseen by the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB). A private business such as Lantern is usually audited only when a lender, investor or regulator requires it.

scenes.head: The second safeguard is professional ethics.

segs.say: The second safeguard is professional ethics. Certified public accountants in the United States follow the AICPA’s Code of Professional Conduct, whose principles include integrity, objectivity and independence, and due care; an auditor must be independent of the company audited, both in fact and in appearance. Ethics binds every accountant, not only auditors. A bookkeeper who records an owner’s holiday as a business expense, or books next month’s sales this month to meet a target, breaks faithful representation and the trust of every user who relies on the numbers.

scenes.head: What does Lantern record?

segs.say: During March, five things happen that involve Lantern. Decide which ones Lantern records in its accounts, and name the assumption or principle that decides each case. (a) Ana invests $20,000 of her savings in exchange for common stock. (b) Ana buys groceries for her family with her personal debit card. (c) A hotel signs an agreement for Lantern to cater its June conference for $5,000, payable after the event; nothing has yet been delivered or paid. (d) Lantern buys an espresso machine and grinder for $12,000, paying $4,000 now and owing the supplier $8,000. (e) A local food blogger praises Lantern’s coffee, and enquiries jump.

scenes.head: What does Lantern record?

segs.say: Step 1. (a) Record it. Money moves from Ana to the company, which under the economic entity assumption is separate from her, so Lantern’s cash rises by $20,000 and so does the owners’ claim on the business. The amount is measured exactly in dollars.
Step 2. (b) Don’t record it. Under the economic entity assumption Lantern’s records contain only Lantern’s events. Ana’s household shopping, paid with her own money, is hers.

Step 3. (c) Don’t record it yet. Nothing has been delivered and no money has changed hands; each side has only promised to act later. Revenue recognition points the same way: Lantern earns the $5,000 when it caters the conference in June. A very large contract might be described in the notes under full disclosure, but it is not an entry in the accounts.
Step 4. (d) Record it, at $12,000. The historical cost principle sets the amount at the price paid, however it is paid: $4,000 in cash now plus $8,000 owed to the supplier.

Step 5. (e) Don’t record it. Under the monetary unit assumption, only events that can be measured reliably in money enter the accounts. The praise may well raise future revenue, and that revenue will be recorded when it is earned.

scenes.head: What does Lantern record?

segs.say: Lantern records (a) and (d). It records nothing for (b), (c) or (e).

The accounts are deliberately narrow: they hold the business’s own events, measured in money. That is what makes them reliable, and it is also why they never tell the whole story of a business. Ana knows the blogger’s praise matters; the accounts will show it only when it turns into revenue.

scenes.head: Is the error material?

segs.say: Suppose that after Lantern’s March statements were prepared, Ana found a $150 repair bill for March that had never been recorded. Lantern had reported net income of $990. Separately, a fictional hotel group, Tidewater Hotels, reported net income of $1,500,000 for its year and then found $60,000 of unrecorded expenses. Its bank loan requires net income of at least $1,480,000. Is each error material?

scenes.head: Is the error material?

segs.say: Step 1. Lantern, size: the error is 150 ÷ 990 ≈ 0.152, or about 15.2% of net income, roughly three times a 5% rule of thumb.

Step 2. Lantern, judgement: a reader comparing months, or the bank checking profit, would see a profit about 15% higher than the true one. The error is material and the statements should be corrected: net income becomes 990 − 150 = 840.
Step 3. Tidewater, size: 60,000 ÷ 1,500,000 = 0.04, or 4%. On size alone, being below a 5% rule of thumb, the error might be presumed immaterial.

Step 4. Tidewater, nature: corrected net income is 1,500,000 − 60,000 = 1,440,000, which is $40,000 below the bank’s $1,480,000 condition. The error decides whether the group complies with its loan agreement, one of the qualitative factors the SEC staff lists. It is material despite being under 5%.

scenes.head: Is the error material?

segs.say: Both errors are material: Lantern’s because of its size relative to profit (about 15%), Tidewater’s because, at only 4% of profit, it still hides a breach of the bank’s condition.

Materiality is judged against a particular business and the decisions of its readers, not against a fixed dollar amount, and a percentage is a starting point, never the conclusion. The $150 that matters at Lantern would be invisible at Tidewater; the $60,000 that looks small at Tidewater matters because of what it hides.

chapters.title: Example: Which statement answers Ana’s question?

scenes.head: Which statement answers Ana’s question?

segs.say: It is early April, and Ana has three questions about March. (1) Did Lantern make money? (2) Can it pay what it owes over the coming months, including the $8,000 still due to the equipment supplier on 2 April? (3) Lantern’s cash rose by $26,650 in March: was that the business’s own doing? Using the March figures in the table under “The four financial statements at a glance”, say which statement answers each question, and what the answer is.

scenes.head: Which statement answers Ana’s question?

segs.say: Step 1. (1) Profit over a period is the income statement’s question. Revenue of $7,100 minus expenses of $6,110 gives net income of $990: yes, a small profit.

Step 2. (2) What the business has and owes at a moment is the balance sheet’s question. At 31 March Lantern holds $26,650 of cash. The amounts it owes that fall due within the next year total $11,810, including $8,760 owed to suppliers; the $10,000 bank note is not due until later. Cash alone covers those near-term debts more than twice: 26,650 ÷ 11,810 ≈ 2.26.

Step 3. (3) Where cash came from is the statement of cash flows’ question. Operating activities added only $950; Ana’s investment and the bank loan, less the $300 dividend, added $29,700 (financing); buying equipment used $4,000 (investing). Together: 950 − 4,000 + 29,700 = 26,650.
Step 4. The statement of changes in equity adds the last piece: of the $990 earned, $300 was paid out as a dividend and $690 kept in the business.

scenes.head: Which statement answers Ana’s question?

segs.say: (1) Income statement: yes, net income of $990. (2) Balance sheet: yes, $26,650 of cash against $11,810 due within a year. (3) Statement of cash flows: mostly not; operations generated only $950 of the $26,650.

No single statement answers every question, which is why a complete set has four. Ana’s comfortable bank balance is mostly invested and borrowed money; the business has yet to show that it can generate cash from customers month after month.

scenes.head: Materiality explorer: the same error in different businesses

segs.say: The explorer starts at Lantern’s March profit of $990 and a hypothetical $150 unrecorded expense. Raise the profit and watch the same error shrink as a percentage; raise the error above the profit and watch a reported profit turn into a loss. The percentage is only the first question: read the note to see what to ask next. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: “Accounting is just bookkeeping.”

segs.say: “Accounting is just bookkeeping.”. Bookkeeping, the recording of transactions, is one part of accounting. Deciding what to record and how, checking the records and explaining what they mean for a decision are the rest, and that is where the judgement lies: whether a deposit is revenue yet, whether an error is material, whether a business is still a going concern.

scenes.head: “If the business made a profit, it has that much more cash.”

segs.say: “If the business made a profit, it has that much more cash.”. Profit and cash flow measure different things. Lantern earned $990 in March, but its cash rose by $26,650 because Ana and the bank put money in; in another month a profitable business can run short of cash because its customers have not paid yet. That is why the income statement and the statement of cash flows are separate statements.

scenes.head: “The owner’s money and the business’s money are the same thing.”

segs.say: “The owner’s money and the business’s money are the same thing.”. Under the economic entity assumption they are kept apart, even in a one-person business. Paying a personal bill from the business account does not create a business expense; it moves resources from the business to its owner, and it must be recorded as exactly that.

scenes.head: “US companies can choose GAAP or IFRS, and everyone else uses IFRS.”

segs.say: “US companies can choose GAAP or IFRS, and everyone else uses IFRS.”. The SEC requires US domestic public companies to use US GAAP; it accepts IFRS statements only from foreign private issuers. Elsewhere, each jurisdiction decides. The IFRS Foundation reports that companies in more than 140 jurisdictions are required to use its standards, but which companies must use them, and which may, varies.

scenes.head: “Material means a large dollar amount.”

segs.say: “Material means a large dollar amount.”. Materiality depends on the business and on the nature of the item. $150 is material against Lantern’s $990 monthly profit and immaterial for a hotel group earning millions. A small error is also material if it turns a loss into a profit, masks a trend, decides whether a loan agreement is met or conceals something unlawful.

scenes.head: “The balance sheet shows what the business is worth.”

segs.say: “The balance sheet shows what the business is worth.”. Most assets are recorded at historical cost, and many valuable things, such as a loyal clientele or a strong reputation built up over time, are not recorded at all because they cannot be measured reliably in money. The balance sheet shows what the business has recorded, measured by the rules; what someone would pay for the business is a separate question.

scenes.head: Fernway Apparel, a fictional clothing brand with two shops and an online store, asks Saltmarsh Textiles, a fictional fabric supplier, to let it buy…

segs.say: Fernway Apparel, a fictional clothing brand with two shops and an online store, asks Saltmarsh Textiles, a fictional fabric supplier, to let it buy up to $60,000 of fabric a month on 60-day credit. Saltmarsh’s credit analyst asks for Fernway’s financial statements for its last two years.

scenes.head: The analyst’s first questions are about the statements themselves, not the numbers in them.

segs.say: The analyst’s first questions are about the statements themselves, not the numbers in them. Were they audited, reviewed by an outside accountant, or only prepared by Fernway’s owner? Audited statements are more verifiable, because an independent professional has examined the evidence. How old are they? Statements for a year that ended ten months ago are less timely than she would like, so she also asks for Fernway’s recent monthly management accounts, knowing that those are unaudited and follow no external rules. Were both years prepared on the same basis? If Fernway changed the way it measures its inventory of clothing between the two years, the figures are less comparable, and the notes should say so.

scenes.head: Then she reads the notes, which the full disclosure principle requires.

segs.say: Then she reads the notes, which the full disclosure principle requires. One note says that a $400,000 bank loan falls due in eight months and that Fernway is negotiating to refinance it. That sentence matters more to Saltmarsh than any line of the income statement, because a supplier selling on 60-day terms is a creditor too: if the bank is not repaid, suppliers may not be either. She checks whether the auditor’s report or the notes mention substantial doubt about Fernway’s ability to continue as a going concern. They don’t, but she asks to see the bank’s refinancing offer before deciding.

scenes.head: Finally, she judges what is material to her own decision.

segs.say: Finally, she judges what is material to her own decision. Fernway’s net income fell from $310,000 to $180,000, which looks alarming, but the notes show that $95,000 of the fall came from the one-off cost of closing a third shop; without it, net income would have been $275,000. She approves credit of $40,000 a month rather than $60,000, with a review in six months, when the refinancing should be settled.

scenes.head: Inside a business the same records serve managerial decisions, under different rules.

segs.say: Inside a business the same records serve managerial decisions, under different rules. The manager of a fictional 120-room hotel deciding whether to close its restaurant on Mondays needs the restaurant’s Monday revenue, the food and staff costs that closing would save, and nonfinancial facts such as how many guests eat in on Mondays. No GAAP applies: her report only has to be relevant and accurate enough for that one decision.

scenes.head: What to remember

segs.say: Accounting identifies a business’s economic events, records them in money and communicates the results to people who make decisions.
Internal users (owners and managers) and external users (investors, lenders, suppliers, customers, employees, tax authorities and regulators) read the same records for different decisions.
Financial accounting serves outsiders under US GAAP or IFRS; managerial accounting serves insiders with no imposed rules; tax accounting follows tax law.
The income statement, statement of changes in equity, balance sheet and statement of cash flows each answer a different question, and profit is not the same as cash.
In the United States the FASB sets GAAP, which the SEC recognises for public companies; the IASB sets IFRS, which companies in more than 140 jurisdictions are required to use.

Useful information is relevant (including material) and faithfully represented (complete, neutral and free from error), and is made more useful by comparability, verifiability, timeliness and understandability, at a cost the benefits justify.

Four assumptions (economic entity, going concern, monetary unit, time period) and four principles (historical cost, revenue recognition, expense recognition, full disclosure) shape what is recorded; audits and professional ethics make the result trustworthy.

scenes.head: Work the guided problems, then take the knowledge check.

segs.say: That is the whole lesson. Now work the guided problems, with hints when you need them, then try the questions on your own and take the knowledge check. A score of 80 percent completes the lesson.
